For a number of reasons, BSD is relatively unknown:

The BSD developers are often more interested in polishing their code than marketing it.

Much of Linux's popularity is due to factors external to the Linux projects, such as the press, and to companies formed to provide Linux services. Until recently, the open source BSDs had no such proponents.

BSD developers tend to be more experienced than Linux developers, and have less interest in making the system easy to use. Newcomers tend to feel more comfortable with Linux.

In 1992, AT&T sued BSDI, the vendor of BSD/386, alleging that the product contained AT&T-copyrighted code. The case was settled out of court in 1994, but the spectre of the litigation continues to haunt people. As recently as March 2000 an article published on the web claimed that the court case had been “recently settled”.

One detail that the lawsuit did clarify is the naming: in the 1980s, BSD was known as “BSD UNIX®”. With the elimination of the last vestige of AT&T code from BSD, it also lost the right to the name UNIX®. Thus you will see references in book titles to “the 4.3BSD UNIX® operating system” and “the 4.4BSD operating system”.

There is a perception that the BSD projects are fragmented and belligerent. The Wall Street Journal spoke of “balkanization” of the BSD projects. Like the law suit, this perception bases mainly on ancient history.

(source: https://www.freebsd.org/doc/en/articles/explaining-bsd/why-is-bsd-not-better-known.html )

First of all, Linux being decentralized can be a weakness, but it is also a strength. It's one of the reasons why it was so much harder for this shit to go down on it, even in a weakened form. That said, it's actually not quite as splintered as it seems. There are a few major super-distros that almost all the others flow from in one way or another - specifically those are Red Hat and Debian. If you want to use Unix like it was in 1999 (not necessarily a bad thing, and it can be a very good thing, but not where I'd start out with), there's also Slackware.

As for how to start, I would suggest the following:

First of all download VirtualBox and download the ISOs for at least three different Linuxes. I would suggest Mint, Ubuntu MATE and Fedora. There are some privacy issues with Ubuntu that may or may not be resolved (NOTHING like Windows though), and the MATE flavor seems to have those problems removed, and I think MATE would be easier for you to adapt to than Unity. Mint you may want to get both the Cinnamon and MATE versions so you can see how two different versions of the same distribution work.

So that you're aware, Ubuntu is a derivative of Debian, and Mint is a derivative of Ubuntu. Fedora is the open source version of Red Hat.

Familiarize yourself with VirtualBox - it isn't too hard - and boot each of these. Run them in Live mode for a bit, and then try to install them.

Then comes the hard part - stick with it for a few days. Use it for most computing tasks. You're going to have a learning curve even before you get to the command prompt, but most basic tasks can be accomplished without it. Try each flavor and see which one seems to fit your working style the best. If none of them do, try a few more. Unfortunately there are a few I've been hankering to try but I have literally forgotten them right this moment, but OpenSUSE is also good, and @Andman17 sticks up for Elementary OS (which I think was one of the ones I wanted to try, no less). Also consider Knoppix, which is fast, relatively friendly, and designed to be used straight off the CD. It's fantastic for emergencies, actually.

Realize however that you are NOT going to be able to play many modern games well in VirtualBox, unless you want to tweak the hell out of it, and even then your results may not be very good at all. You WILL run into performance issues on VirtualBox. This is the nature of the beast. In the meantime do research to see how well Linux supports your hardware, particularly if you're interested in video card performance.

After that, try burning some of the CDs or DVDs to disc and boot off of them. This is where Knoppix is particularly handy, but most of the popular Linuxes can work decently enough booting straight off the install CD, and not just in an emergency recovery context, either.

Once you're ready, make the plunge and repartition your hard drive. I would consult the folks over on /v/linux for the details, since I quite frankly haven't made a dual boot system in quite a while. Give Linux a healthy chunk of the drive, and try it out.

Be aware you will probably have to do some tweaking, particularly for video hardware. This will help you get familiar with things such as the command prompt. Note that this does not mean you'll need to tweak a lot to get a usable system, but to get the most out of it, especially video acceleration, you may well have to manually fix some things up. Again, you'll need to do some research, but this may be beneficial in the long run. If you have anything specialized, do not be afraid to look it up by model number or name. In fact, it's best if you do that for all your major hardware components, as well as the computer model itself. There are some with some hardware that just won't work right with the system, unfortunately, but other stuff that's having problems can be made to work well with a few tweaks. Also note that with the video drivers, Linux generally supports the least common denominator well in that department, so don't worry about missing a GUI. That's mostly for graphics acceleration.

Now, let's say you got this far. You want to go further into Linux and move over Windows stuff? There are a few ways you can go. The best known is Wine, which is an open source program and free. I haven't ever had much luck with it but some have had great success with it. If you want something more polished that I had great luck with some time ago, look for CodeWeavers' software. They produce some rather affordable Windows crossover products, which IIRC include a lot of the stuff from Wine and amp it up. You can also run VirtualBox for Linux and install a full-up Windows install there, but remember that at least for Windows 10, Microsoft can see what you're doing in the virtual machine. I don't know how well CodeWeavers' stuff, or Wine, work for Office 365, but for most other Office versions, compatibility with these programs is a major priority so they should probably do pretty well for the most part. Photoshop probably also ranks up there in importance. But as stated, games are not. There are some solutions developing with those, e.g. Steam OS, but it's going to take time. CrossWeavers also, IIRC, has a game-specific package you can buy. I don't know how good it is since I don't play many modern games, but it certainly LOOKS like it's able to do things pretty well.

In terms of "call for help," well, there isn't all that much you can do for a lot of software, either. The fallback with computer problems these days tends to be forums, and Linux is moreso with that. I would not agree with @Tabarnak, as a Red Hat subscription is, to the best of my knowledge, ridiculously expensive. However, many Linux communities are friendly and there are a lot of them that are quite willing to help out newbies. Many have extensive wikis that can answer most questions on their own. With some of them, they include the exact thing you need to copy and paste into a terminal, reducing relatively technical instructions to a copy-and-paste operation.

One thing to be wary of - and nowhere near enough people are talking about this - is that with the UEFI bullshit, Microsoft is slowly pushing in the direction of making it much harder to boot up Linux, unless you're running a bootloader and/or kernel approved by Microsoft. I suspect that the other shoe on that will drop quite horribly in due time, if it ends up going to its full extent unchecked, and it very well might. As such you'll do better on some older hardware most likely.

One other thing - there are some distros you should avoid. This is because a lot of them are super-specialized, and others are for users that are very advanced. Gentoo, for instance, literally exists so people can recompile the entire system to their specifications themselves, and ArchLinux is a highly technical one too. Slackware, while highly versatile, is probably not the best for someone who wants an easy introduction into Linux. Kali Linux is based around security. Debian is an extremely important one, but IMO it's a bit much for a new user compared to some of its derivatives. And there are others along those lines as well, but the "mainstream" ones should do pretty good.

I will warn you that in terms of programming I don't think Visual Basic will do all that well for Linux. While you can certainly try to run it, and Mono is out there (.NET for Linux, IIRC), it's not going to be the easiest thing around. If you want to go that route I would strongly recommend using it in VirtualBox. Additionally, don't count on the software thus produced to necessarily run on Linux. If you're interested in Linux development there are other options. C/C++ is the classic Unix programming language. Java is up there as well and has some decent IDEs. There are also scripting languages such as Python and Perl that are rather popular. Unfortunately BASIC itself is not terribly well represented so you'll have to learn some more there, but it's probably easier than it seems to pick up at least the basics (although GUI programming will definitely be more difficult, in no small part because VB is designed explicitly to hide the worst of the messiness of putting together a working UI).

In any case, I wish you luck. Hopefully this will help you some.

"Finally, we will access, disclose and preserve personal data, including your content (such as the content of your emails, other private communications or files in private folders), when we have a good faith belief that doing so is necessary to:

operate and maintain the security of our services, including to prevent or stop an attack on our computer systems or networks or protect the rights or property of Microsoft, including enforcing the terms governing the use of the services - however, if we receive information indicating that someone is using our services to traffic in stolen intellectual or physical property of Microsoft, we will not inspect a customer's private content ourselves, but we may refer the matter to law enforcement."

This does not give bulk collection rights, but it does mean if there is a warrant for someone, they can give up the data. They can also get into a scammer's PC and find out where they are based. So if there is no warrant for you and you are not illegally distributing MS IP or running a phone-scam center, there is nothing to worry about.

Good faith belief means true belief. This means only if they truly think collection is necessary will they actually disclose the data. Belief is an actual state of mind. If you pretend to believe, then you aren't believing. This is not bulk collection.

Let's break down what the official page on Windows 10 privacy says (the one linked to from the user agreement):

Activation: totally fine, only sends activation key if necessary.

Advertising ID: easy to opt-out, same practice as other advertising companies

Input Personalization: "You can turn off Input Personalization at any time. This will stop the data collection for this feature and will delete associated data stored on your device"

Location Services: Send location info to MS, but can easily be turned off.

Security and Safety features:

  • Device Encryption: Bitlocker key is automatically backed up on OneDrive. 2 reasons this is not an issue: 1, it doesn't mean sending the data on the hdd to MS, it only means sending the key. A key is useless without the data. 2, if you are a target for law enforcement, a key won't stop the gov't from forcing you to enter the key. In short, no problems caused by this.
  • Malware Removal Tool: "If you do not want MSRT to send this data to Microsoft, you can disable MSRT's reporting component. "
  • Microsoft Family: Essentially, MS data mining this is the parents fault. MS is only giving the option to track.
  • SmartScreen: SmartScreen can be turned off, but the data sending to MS is necessary to check the program without having a huge database on the PC wasting space.
  • Defender: same deal as Malware Removal Tool

Sync Settings: only applies to MS accounts, MS accounts can still disable a lot

Telemetry: If set to basic, MS gets the PC specs, what is installed (so they know if you have Tor if it's installed, but not what you do on it), and if your PC is working correctly (yes-no, not a huge concern). Enhanced sees how often you use said programs, but not what you do on them. Full gets system files, so and memory snapshots. This is only if a program crashes, but it could contain stuff you were doing when it crashed, but not your documents on your HDD.

  • Error Reporting: This will however send "files that help describe the problem." This is a little broad, but error means an accident, so something you accessed on purpose could not be considered an "error," and it would only be files that "describe the problem" so they can't just get bank statements if MS word crashed, unless you happened to have your finances in the word document.

Updates: Essentially just installs new fixes and possibly new software, however this software still has to comply with the privacy policy, so it is not worrisome. People should be updating their PCs anyway, so I think this is a step in the right direction.

Edge and IE: only new privacy issues are if you have Cortana, Page predictions, or suggested sites, otherwise after disabling this, privacy is the same as any browser except for the lack of extensions (lack of extensions is a big one, but it's not MS's fault since it was rushed) Wifi Sense: If MS has your wifi, as long as you have HTTPS, MS can't just use a snoop beacon to catch your traffic. Wifi passwords are not actually that big of an issue. It's not necessarily what MS does, but whatever friends do on the network. IP related liability is pretty low, otherwise hola users would be in trouble, and there has not been a single criminal case against an hola user. I don't think it's anything to worry about (heck I have an open hotspot, it really doesn't matter much)

Windows apps: all can be turned off through privacy panel

Windows Hello: opt-in, requires special hardware anyway

Store: no privacy issues, but walled gardens suck, and it's littered with ads, so stay away anyway.
